A firefighter $F$ is lowering a rescue basket $B$ from a helicopter. The basket stays $40\,\text{ft}$ above the ground while it moves horizontally toward the firefighter at a speed of $12\,\text{ft/s}.$ Find, in radians per second as a function of $\theta ,$ the rate at which the angle $\theta $ between the cable and the horizontal is increasing.

The angle is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
$\text{rad/s}.$
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14232470/assets/cfac2040d258398133397c5322e650bf60f59c7c372c97bfecec654eb3a4a278.png)

In the figure, $y$ is the basket's height, and $x$ is the horizontal distance between the firefighter and the basket. The quantity $y=40$ feet does not change with time because the basket height remains the same.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $x$ and $y$ are the adjacent and opposite, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{40}{x} \\ x & =40\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(40\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(-40{csc}^{2}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-12\,\text{ft/s}$ (negative because the horizontal distance is decreasing). Substituting this into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}-12 & =(-40{csc}^{2}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{12}{40} & =({csc}^{2}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =\frac{12}{40}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =\frac{3}{10}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the angle is increasing at a rate of $\frac{3}{10}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{rad/s}.$
